title: Were Ancient Humans STRONGER Than Us?
title_alternatives: Stone Age vs Today: Who Was Really STRONGER?
Why Ancient Women Had Stronger Arms Than ROWERS
Why Are Our BONES So Light?
description:
Her arm bones were stronger than a rower's. This video asks whether ancient humans were really stronger than us, using bone studies of early farmers and foragers, the Neandertal debate, the chimp strength myth, grip strength today and the world deadlift record.

This video is history and science, not medical or fitness advice.

Sources:
- Macintosh, Pinhasi & Stock (2017). Science Advances.
- Ryan & Shaw (2015). PNAS.
- Ruff et al. (2015). PNAS.
- Chirchir et al. (2015). PNAS.
- O'Neill et al. (2017). PNAS.
- Fain & Weatherford (2016). Journal of Hand Therapy.

O'Neill et al. (2017). Chimpanzee super strength and human skeletal muscle evolution. PNAS 114, 7343-7348
Ryan & Shaw (2015). Gracility of the modern Homo sapiens skeleton is the result of decreased biomechanical loading. PNAS 112, 372-377
Fain & Weatherford (2016). Comparative study of millennials' (age 20-34 years) grip and lateral pinch with the norms. Journal of Hand Therapy 29, 483-488
Guinness World Records, heaviest deadlift (501 kg, Hafthor Bjornsson, 2 May 2020; Eddie Hall was first past 500 kg in 2016)
Ruff et al. (2015). Gradual decline in mobility with the adoption of food production in Europe. PNAS 112, 7147-7152

Berger & Trinkaus (1995). Patterns of trauma among the Neandertals. Journal of Archaeological Science 22, 841-852

scenes.narration: Her arm bones were stronger than a rower's.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character flexes one arm next to a long wooden rowing oar, wide-eyed and surprised.

scenes.narration: Neolithic women in Central Europe beat modern athletes.
scenes.image_prompt: Two ancient arm bones side by side on a flat stone, one clearly thicker than the other, soft light.
scenes.fact_source: Macintosh, Pinhasi & Stock (2017). Prehistoric women's manual labor exceeded that of athletes through the first 5500 years of farming in Central Europe. Science Advances 3, eaao3893

scenes.narration: So were ancient humans simply stronger than us?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character looks at his own thin arm, then at a huge round boulder, puzzled.

scenes.narration: Chimps aren't ten times stronger than you. Not even close.
scenes.image_prompt: A chimpanzee sitting calmly on the ground next to a thick rope and a wooden handle.
scenes.fact_source: O'Neill et al. (2017). Chimpanzee super strength and human skeletal muscle evolution. PNAS 114, 7343-7348

scenes.narration: Because the answer says something about your own body.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character pokes his own upper arm and looks down at it, curious.

scenes.narration: Forager hip bones were as sturdy as other primates'.
scenes.image_prompt: A cross-section of a hip joint bone showing a fine inner lattice, drawn simply on a plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Ryan & Shaw (2015). Gracility of the modern Homo sapiens skeleton is the result of decreased biomechanical loading. PNAS 112, 372-377

scenes.narration: By the end, you'll know who really wins.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character crosses his arms with a confident grin, one eyebrow raised.

scenes.narration: Young adults' grip tested weaker than nineteen eighty-five norms.
scenes.image_prompt: A hand squeezing a simple spring hand-grip tool against a plain pale background.
scenes.fact_source: Fain & Weatherford (2016). Comparative study of millennials' (age 20-34 years) grip and lateral pinch with the norms. Journal of Hand Therapy 29, 483-488

scenes.narration: Is that progress, or something we quietly lost?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a heavy rock in both hands, strains, then looks at his palms.

scenes.narration: Guinness lists a deadlift of five hundred and one kilograms.
scenes.image_prompt: A huge barbell loaded with big round plates resting on a plain floor.
scenes.fact_source: Guinness World Records, heaviest deadlift (501 kg, Hafthor Bjornsson, 2 May 2020; Eddie Hall was first past 500 kg in 2016)

scenes.narration: So who wins, the ancient hunter or the modern lifter?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands between a hunter holding a spear and an athlete holding a barbell, looking from one to the other.

scenes.narration: Something changed in our legs when farming began.
scenes.image_prompt: A single long leg bone lying on dry ground between a wheat stalk and a wooden spear, no people.
scenes.fact_source: Ruff et al. (2015). Gradual decline in mobility with the adoption of food production in Europe. PNAS 112, 7147-7152

scenes.narration: Quick honesty first. Nobody has ever measured an ancient person's muscles. Muscle doesn't fossilize, so everything here is read from bones.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a long old bone up to the light like a detective, squinting at it.

scenes.narration: The idea is simple. Bone responds to the loads it carries, so thick, strong bones point to a physically demanding life.
scenes.image_prompt: Two bone cross-sections side by side, one thick-walled and one thin-walled, on a plain pale background.
scenes.fact_source: Ryan & Shaw (2015). Gracility of the modern Homo sapiens skeleton is the result of decreased biomechanical loading. PNAS 112, 372-377

scenes.narration: It's like reading someone's shoes. Worn heels, lots of walking. Mine mostly say I walk to the fridge.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds up a badly worn sandal, inspecting the heel closely, grinning.

scenes.narration: Alison Macintosh's team CT-scanned the arm and leg bones of living women, from runners and rowers to sedentary people, and compared them with early farmers from Central Europe.
scenes.image_prompt: A small tabletop scanner with a long arm bone resting inside its round opening.
scenes.fact_source: Macintosh, Pinhasi & Stock (2017). Prehistoric women's manual labor exceeded that of athletes through the first 5500 years of farming in Central Europe. Science Advances 3, eaao3893

scenes.narration: So, who had the strongest arms? Take a guess. I'll wait.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character taps his chin, thinking, beside three figures: one holding an oar, one running, one sitting.

scenes.narration: The early farming women's arm bones were eleven to sixteen percent stronger for their size than the rowers', and almost thirty percent stronger than typical Cambridge students'.
scenes.image_prompt: Two ancient arm bones next to a modern rowing oar on a stone surface, soft light.
scenes.fact_source: Macintosh, Pinhasi & Stock (2017). Prehistoric women's manual labor exceeded that of athletes through the first 5500 years of farming in Central Europe. Science Advances 3, eaao3893

scenes.narration: Not stronger than office workers. Stronger than people who row for a living. So what was she doing all day?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands with arms out, mouth open in amazement, in front of a field of golden wheat.

scenes.narration: The team suggested grinding grain by hand on a stone, for hours, as one possible cause. But they said they couldn't name the exact behavior.
scenes.image_prompt: A flat stone slab with a smaller stone on top and a pile of golden grain beside it, close up.
scenes.fact_source: Macintosh, Pinhasi & Stock (2017). Prehistoric women's manual labor exceeded that of athletes through the first 5500 years of farming in Central Europe. Science Advances 3, eaao3893

scenes.narration: Before we crown anyone, notice something. These were farmers, not hunters, and they weren't superheroes from head to toe.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a small crown above the head of a farmer figure, then pauses, unsure.

scenes.narration: Their shin bones looked a lot like those of sedentary women on average, and were weaker than those of living runners and football players.
scenes.image_prompt: Two long shin bones on a stone, one thick and one slim, side by side, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Macintosh, Pinhasi & Stock (2017). Prehistoric women's manual labor exceeded that of athletes through the first 5500 years of farming in Central Europe. Science Advances 3, eaao3893

scenes.narration: So what about people who hunted and gathered, and walked everywhere?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character walks across a dry savanna with a walking stick, tall grass around him, determined.

scenes.narration: Timothy Ryan and Colin Shaw compared the inner hip bone of four recent human groups and some other primates. Foragers' hips were comparable to similar-sized primates' and clearly stronger than those of sedentary farmers.
scenes.image_prompt: A cross-section of a hip joint bone showing a fine inner lattice, drawn simply on a plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Ryan & Shaw (2015). Gracility of the modern Homo sapiens skeleton is the result of decreased biomechanical loading. PNAS 112, 372-377

scenes.narration: So a forager's hips were built like a primate's, and mine are built for sitting. I'm choosing not to take that personally.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sits sunk deep in a soft cushioned armchair, completely relaxed, eyes half closed.

scenes.narration: Their data best supported low physical activity as the reason modern skeletons are lighter, though they noted that a grain-heavy diet might play a part too.
scenes.image_prompt: A balance scale with a small wheat bundle on one side and a bone on the other, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Ryan & Shaw (2015). Gracility of the modern Homo sapiens skeleton is the result of decreased biomechanical loading. PNAS 112, 372-377

scenes.narration: So lighter bones aren't a law of nature. They look more like the result of how we live.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character looks at a long bone in his hand, thinking, in warm light.

scenes.narration: Habiba Chirchir's team measured the spongy bone inside limb joints in people, chimps and fossils. Only recent humans had low density throughout the limbs.
scenes.image_prompt: A cross-section of a knee joint bone with a delicate honeycomb pattern inside, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Chirchir et al. (2015). Recent origin of low trabecular bone density in modern humans. PNAS 112, 366-371

scenes.narration: Recent. That's the word that matters. Not a million years of evolution. Just the last few thousand years of how we live.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands beside a very long timeline strip drawn on the ground, pointing to the last tiny piece.

scenes.narration: The drop was biggest in the hip, knee and ankle, and smaller in the shoulder, elbow and hand.
scenes.image_prompt: Three joint bones in a row, hip, knee and ankle, drawn simply on a plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Chirchir et al. (2015). Recent origin of low trabecular bone density in modern humans. PNAS 112, 366-371

scenes.narration: Legs lose the most. Honestly, that tracks. My legs mostly commute between the bed and the couch.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character lies stretched on a couch with both tired legs up in the air, grinning.

scenes.narration: A study of more than eighteen hundred skeletons across Europe, from the Ice Age to the twentieth century, found a large drop in leg bone strength that began with the Neolithic.
scenes.image_prompt: A long row of many leg bones laid out in order across a pale surface, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Ruff et al. (2015). Gradual decline in mobility with the adoption of food production in Europe. PNAS 112, 7147-7152

scenes.narration: Not the smartphone. Not the office chair. It began when people settled down to farm.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands at the edge of a small wheat field next to a simple hut, looking out.

scenes.narration: Arm bones changed much less, and less consistently. The big loss was in how well the leg bones resisted front-to-back bending, which the authors read as less walking.
scenes.image_prompt: An arm bone and a leg bone side by side on a pale plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Ruff et al. (2015). Gradual decline in mobility with the adoption of food production in Europe. PNAS 112, 7147-7152

scenes.narration: Quick pause. If this is making you curious, subscribe and stay with me. We're going to keep digging into the human story together, one strange question at a time. It's free, it takes a second, and it helps more curious people find the channel.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character waves at the viewer with a friendly smile, standing in a sunny field.

scenes.narration: Now the Neandertals. Steven Churchill and Jill Rhodes studied the muscle attachment sites and leverage in their arms, and argued for pronounced upper-body strength compared with most modern humans.
scenes.image_prompt: A thick fossil arm bone with a prominent ridge on it, lit softly on a stone.
scenes.fact_source: Churchill & Rhodes (2006). How strong were the Neandertals? Leverage and muscularity at the shoulder and elbow in Mousterian foragers. Periodicum Biologorum 108

scenes.narration: Picture hunting a big animal with a spear in your hand, not thrown from far away. You'd want serious shoulders.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character braces with a long wooden spear held in both hands, wide-eyed, facing the huge shadow of an animal.

scenes.narration: In nineteen ninety-five, Berger and Trinkaus noticed that Neandertal skeletons showed many head and neck injuries, a pattern like rodeo riders', and linked it to hunting up close.
scenes.image_prompt: A fossil skull with a healed dent on its forehead resting on a rock in dim light.
scenes.fact_source: Berger & Trinkaus (1995). Patterns of trauma among the Neandertals. Journal of Archaeological Science 22, 841-852

scenes.narration: Rodeo riders. Meanwhile, I once pulled a muscle opening a pickle jar.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character wearing a cowboy hat with a bandage on his head, holding a rope, dizzy but proud.

scenes.narration: But in twenty eighteen, Judith Beier, Katerina Harvati and colleagues compared several hundred fossil skulls and found that Neandertals and early modern humans had similar rates of head injuries.
scenes.image_prompt: Two fossil skulls side by side on a flat rock, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Beier, Anthes, Wahl & Harvati (2018). Similar cranial trauma prevalence among Neanderthals and Upper Palaeolithic modern humans. Nature 563, 686-690

scenes.narration: So the rodeo story has a crack in it. Maybe Neandertals simply lived as dangerously as everyone else back then.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a small cracked clay plate, running a finger along the crack, thoughtful.

scenes.narration: Colin Shaw's team also tested the spear idea. They put sensors on volunteers' arm muscles. Spear thrusting loaded the non-dominant arm more, but scraping a hide loaded the dominant arm, closer to what the bones show.
scenes.image_prompt: A stretched animal hide on a wooden frame with a stone scraper lying on it, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Shaw, Hofmann, Petraglia, Stock & Gottschall (2012). Neandertal humeri may reflect adaptation to scraping tasks, but not spear thrusting. PLoS ONE 7(7): e40349

scenes.narration: So maybe the real Neandertal workout wasn't wrestling mammoths. It was cleaning animal hides. Nobody puts that on a poster.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character scrapes a stretched hide on a wooden frame with a stone tool, sweating hard.

scenes.narration: Now the chimp myth. Popular claims say they're five or ten times stronger than us. A careful review of the data found chimp muscle performs about one and a half times better.
scenes.image_prompt: A chimpanzee hanging from a thick tree branch by one arm, calm.
scenes.fact_source: O'Neill et al. (2017). Chimpanzee super strength and human skeletal muscle evolution. PNAS 114, 7343-7348

scenes.narration: One and a half times. I'd still lose the arm wrestle. Honestly, I'd lose to most of my friends too.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character and a chimpanzee arm wrestling on a small tree stump table, the main character sweating, the chimp relaxed.

scenes.narration: Their simulations gave one point three five times. The gap comes mostly from fast-twitch fibers, and they suggest human muscle shifted toward cheap, repetitive movement, like walking.
scenes.image_prompt: A chimpanzee silhouette leaping between two branches beside a long footpath winding into the distance.
scenes.fact_source: O'Neill et al. (2017). Chimpanzee super strength and human skeletal muscle evolution. PNAS 114, 7343-7348

scenes.narration: So we traded explosive power for stamina. Like swapping a sports car for really good walking shoes.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character happily holds a pair of sturdy walking sandals while a tiny toy sports car sits abandoned behind him.

scenes.narration: Now the other direction. A twenty sixteen study of two hundred and thirty-seven adults aged twenty to thirty-four found grip strength below nineteen eighty-five norms. Men twenty to twenty-four averaged about one hundred and one pounds in the right hand, versus one hundred and twenty-one.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple spring hand-grip tool with a gauge, resting on a plain wooden table.
scenes.fact_source: Fain & Weatherford (2016). Comparative study of millennials' (age 20-34 years) grip and lateral pinch with the norms. Journal of Hand Therapy 29, 483-488

scenes.narration: My hands mostly do one job: scroll. Let's not test my grip today.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a flat glowing slab in one hand, thumb scrolling, the other arm hanging limp.

scenes.narration: Grip isn't just a party trick, either. In the PURE study of about one hundred and forty thousand adults in seventeen countries, each five-kilogram drop in grip strength went with about sixteen percent higher risk of death from any cause.
scenes.image_prompt: A strong hand gripping a thick rope tightly, close up, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Leong et al. (2015). Prognostic value of grip strength: findings from the Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology (PURE) study. The Lancet 386, 266-273

scenes.narration: Now, that's a link, not proof. A weak grip doesn't cause anything on its own.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character looks at a small glowing warning lamp on a stone panel, arms crossed, thoughtful.

scenes.narration: It predicted death more strongly than systolic blood pressure did. Even so, the lead author said more research is needed on whether building strength actually lowers anyone's risk.
scenes.image_prompt: A rubber blood pressure bulb and cuff lying beside a hand-grip tool on a table, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Leong et al. (2015). Prognostic value of grip strength: findings from the Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology (PURE) study. The Lancet 386, 266-273

scenes.narration: I'm not a doctor, and this isn't advice. I'm just telling you the story the bones tell.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character raises both palms in a calm gesture, shaking his head gently, in warm light.

scenes.narration: And yet at the very top, we are stronger than ever. Eddie Hall was first past five hundred kilograms in twenty sixteen. Hafthor Bjornsson lifted five hundred and one in twenty twenty, according to Guinness.
scenes.image_prompt: A huge barbell loaded with big round plates resting on a plain floor.
scenes.fact_source: Guinness World Records, heaviest deadlift (501 kg, Hafthor Bjornsson, 2 May 2020; Eddie Hall was first past 500 kg in 2016)

scenes.narration: Five hundred and one kilograms is about the weight of a horse. I can barely lift my suitcase at the airport.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands tiny under a giant loaded barbell, a calm horse standing patiently beside it.

scenes.narration: Notice the comparison in the rowing study, though. The rowers were semi-elite athletes who train on purpose. The farming women's arm pattern most resembled theirs, with no training plan at all.
scenes.image_prompt: A wooden rowing boat with two oars resting on a calm shore next to a stone grinding slab, evening light.
scenes.fact_source: Macintosh, Pinhasi & Stock (2017). Prehistoric women's manual labor exceeded that of athletes through the first 5500 years of farming in Central Europe. Science Advances 3, eaao3893

scenes.narration: So 'stronger' can mean three things: the biggest single lift, the toughness of an everyday body, or stamina over a long day. Ancient people clearly won the second.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character counts on three raised fingers, one eyebrow lifted, in front of a blank stone wall.

scenes.narration: Ryan and Shaw also tested the other explanations: that human bone biology is just different from other primates, or that our big joint surfaces spread the load. Neither fit the data.
scenes.image_prompt: A large joint surface of a hip bone next to a small joint surface of another primate's bone, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Ryan & Shaw (2015). Gracility of the modern Homo sapiens skeleton is the result of decreased biomechanical loading. PNAS 112, 372-377

scenes.narration: That's the surprising part. Lighter bones don't seem to be about being human. They're about what our bones are asked to do.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character carries a bundle of firewood on his shoulder up a grassy hill, smiling.

scenes.narration: To be fair, the grip study has critics. Some experts said the sample was small and wanted a follow-up, especially since only four men were in the thirty to thirty-four group.
scenes.image_prompt: Four small pebbles sitting alone on a large flat stone, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Fain & Weatherford (2016). Comparative study of millennials' (age 20-34 years) grip and lateral pinch with the norms. Journal of Hand Therapy 29, 483-488

scenes.narration: I like that. A study that points out its own weak spots is a study I trust more.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character gives a thumbs up beside a scroll with a small dent drawn in it, smiling.

scenes.narration: The bone density researchers noted that early members of our species, around twenty thousand years ago, still had bone about as dense as other primates.
scenes.image_prompt: A pale fossil hip bone and a primate hip bone side by side on a flat stone, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Chirchir et al. (2015). Recent origin of low trabecular bone density in modern humans. PNAS 112, 366-371

scenes.narration: A teenager from twenty thousand years ago had hips built like a primate's. I get winded carrying groceries up one flight.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character struggles up a short staircase carrying a big pile of baskets, panting.

scenes.narration: Back to the women in Central Europe. Bronze Age women had arm bones nine to thirteen percent stronger than the rowers', but leg bones about twelve percent weaker.
scenes.image_prompt: Two long bones, one thick arm bone and one slimmer leg bone, on a flat stone.
scenes.fact_source: Macintosh, Pinhasi & Stock (2017). Prehistoric women's manual labor exceeded that of athletes through the first 5500 years of farming in Central Europe. Science Advances 3, eaao3893

scenes.narration: So the strongest arms in the study came with unremarkable legs. Strong at what? It depends on the job.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character carries a heavy basket on his head with strong arms but wobbly legs, comically.

scenes.narration: The authors called the transition gradual: mobility first fell as food production began, and kept falling as farming intensified.
scenes.image_prompt: A long winding footpath that grows fainter as it nears a wheat field, plain background, no people.
scenes.fact_source: Ruff et al. (2015). Gradual decline in mobility with the adoption of food production in Europe. PNAS 112, 7147-7152

scenes.narration: So who wins? Ancient people had sturdier bones because daily life loaded them. We win at the peak: the biggest lift, the best food, the best training.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a balance scale with a sturdy thick bone on one side and a small barbell on the other.

scenes.narration: The same European study found no clear change in the last two thousand years. So machines and cities mattered less than the shift to farming.
scenes.image_prompt: A tall clay water jug next to an old stone road and a wheat bundle, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Ruff et al. (2015). Gradual decline in mobility with the adoption of food production in Europe. PNAS 112, 7147-7152

scenes.narration: Which means this isn't a failure. It's a trade we made for farms, cities and medicine, and our bones quietly paid part of the price.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character weighs a small bone against a loaf of bread on a balance scale, thoughtful.

scenes.narration: The authors tied that late shift to settled life and our growing reliance on technology and culture.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple stone house beside a wheat field with a thin bone resting on its doorstep, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Chirchir et al. (2015). Recent origin of low trabecular bone density in modern humans. PNAS 112, 366-371

scenes.narration: So, were ancient humans stronger than us? In bone and everyday toughness, often yes. At the peak, no. Our bones build themselves around whatever life asks of them. Thanks for hanging out with me for these minutes. Hit like if it was worth your time, and tell me in the comments which kind of strong you'd rather be. I read every one. Next time: what could ancient humans do that we can't? See you soon, friend.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character waves goodbye at sunrise beside a small campfire, a bright sky behind him, smiling warmly.
